extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and other Office personnel (and patent practitioners seeking to understand USPTO obviousness practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for USPTO personnel on evaluating and articulating obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including the Graham factual inquiries, search scope, level of ordinary skill, permissible rationales, and how to consider applicant rebuttal and secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is a question of law based on underlying factual inquiries enunciated in Graham: (A) determining the scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art. Objective evidence (secondary considerations) must be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Graham factors as the controlling inquiries in any obviousness analysis; sequence may be reordered in particular cases. Evaluate secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt needs, failure of others, unexpected results) on a case-by-case basis and include them in the record when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel factfinding and articulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel act as factfinders and must ensure the written record includes findings of fact concerning the state of the art and teachings of the references applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate factual findings and the rationale(s) supporting an obviousness rejection in the Office action so the applicant is notified of the reasons (35 U.S.C. 132) and can respond. Findings may include how a person of ordinary skill would understand prior art teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the invention by reading the specification and claims, give the claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, then decide what to search for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search should cover the claimed subject matter and disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed. See MPEP §904 for search methodology and MPEP §2111 for claim interpretation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to search for
rubrics_metrics.description: The search should target the claimed subject matter and disclosed features reasonably expected to be claimed, not only literal claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a rejection need not be based on a teaching or suggestion to combine, a preferred search is directed to finding references that provide such a teaching or suggestion if they exist (see MPEP §904.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to search (analogous and nonanalogous art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art for 35 U.S.C. 103 purposes can be in the applicant’s field of endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the particular problem addressed by the applicant; work from other fields may be considered if reasonably pertinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow general search guidelines in MPEP §904 and consider analogous art (see MPEP §2141.01(a)). Per KSR, do not limit searches to only art solving the same problem — design incentives and market forces may make other-field references relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification when determining claim scope for search and comparison purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Phillips v. AWH and MPEP §2111 principles in construing claim language before comparing to prior art; ensure scope determination is clear in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertaining differences between claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret claim language and compare the claimed invention as a whole to the prior art to identify differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both the invention and the prior art as a whole (see MPEP §2141.02). All claim limitations must be considered in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness rejection should include, explicitly or implicitly, an indication of the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; this finding may be used as a basis for resolving obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: (1) type of problems encountered in the art; (2) prior art solutions; (3) rapidity of innovations; (4) sophistication of the technology; and (5) educational level of active workers. The particular factors present will vary; examiners may rely on their technical expertise to describe the knowledge and skills of a person of ordinary skill (In re GPAC, In re Berg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of the person of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of ordinary skill is a hypothetical person presumed to know the relevant art and is a person of ordinary creativity, not an automaton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such a person may fit teachings of multiple patents like pieces of a puzzle, and may employ inferences and creative steps (KSR). Avoid defining the hypothetical person solely by credentials without record support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common sense and examiner expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Common sense and the examiner’s scientific/technical competence may inform what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill, even if not explicitly taught in a particular reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While record support is required, examiners may employ reasoned explanations that use common sense or their expertise to explain why a claimed combination would have been obvious (see DyStar, Perfect Web).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales to support rejections (exemplary list A–G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include: (A) combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) use of known technique to improve similar devices in the same way; (D) applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) 'obvious to try' — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) known work in one field prompting predictable variations in same or different fields; (G) some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is exemplary, not exhaustive. See MPEP §2143 and §2144 for further discussion and examples illustrating each rationale. The key is clearly articulating why the claimed invention would have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art and record establish a teaching, suggestion, or motivation to combine references (TSM), an obviousness rejection using that rationale should be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR cautioned against overly rigid TSM application but recognized it as a valid rationale. Use TSM where appropriate; also consider other rationales. Look for explicit or implicit motivation, including what one of ordinary skill would have understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for articulated reasoning (no conclusory statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning supporting the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit explanation linking factual findings to the legal conclusion (KSR quoting In re Kahn). Avoid conclusory labels — explain why prior art would have motivated or made the claimed combination predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply requirements under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office erred as to factual findings. Mere assertions that the Office has not established a prima facie case or unsupported reliance on common knowledge are substantively inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must consider all timely rebuttal evidence presented by applicants when reevaluating an obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations and may show (A) inability to combine elements by known methods, (B) elements in combination do not merely perform their separate functions, or (C) results were unexpected. Reconsider the entire record and confirm continued viability of rejections before making an action final (see MPEP §706.07(a) and §2145).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence relevant to obviousness — commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected results — must be evaluated and weighed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence may be in the specification, accompany the application, or be provided timely later; weight is case-by-case and presence of evidence is not dispositive by itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-prior-art references to show level of skill or motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: References that are not prior art because they postdate the invention or were not widely disseminated may nonetheless be used to demonstrate the level of ordinary skill in the art or an implicit motivation to combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may cite post-dating documents or otherwise unavailable documents to show what one of ordinary skill would have known or to explain motivation to combine (see Ex parte Erlich; Nat'l Steel Car decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying particular level of skill not always necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If the only facts of record about level of skill are found within the prior art of record, a specific finding of a particular level of skill may not be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the prior art itself reflects an appropriate level of skill, an invention may be held obvious without separately specifying the hypothetical person's exact credentials (Chore-Time, Okajima).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain objectivity by properly ascertaining level of skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolving the level of ordinary skill is necessary to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry and ensure the determination is based on what would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill, not to the inventor, judge, layman, or geniuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the record explains why the selected level of skill is appropriate for the field so that the analysis remains objective and well-founded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred practice to search for teaching/suggestion to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Although rejections need not rely on teaching/suggestion to combine, preferred practice is to search for references that provide such a teaching or suggestion if they exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct searches to find combinations or motivations reflected in prior art; if none exist, provide other reasoned rationales (e.g., predictable results, common sense) with factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory principle: manner of making the invention irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made; obviousness is judged by what would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill at the relevant time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus analysis on prior art, knowledge of one of ordinary skill, and reasonable expectations; the inventor’s method of discovery is not dispositive.
